syllabication of word

description::
· I syllabicate words on vowel.
· example: la-ngu-age, tri-phthong.
[hmnSngo.2019-08-10]
===
"Syllabification (/sɪˌlζbɪfɪˈkeɪʃən/) or syllabication (/sɪˌlζbɪˈkeɪʃən/) is the separation of a word into syllables, whether spoken or written."
[{2019-08-10} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllabification]
"Syllabification is the separation of a word into syllables, whether spoken or written. In most languages, the actually spoken syllables are the basis of syllabification in writing too. Due to the very weak correspondence between sounds and letters in the spelling of modern English, for example, written syllabification in English has to be based mostly on etymological i.e. morphological instead of phonetic principles. English written syllables therefore do not correspond to the actually spoken syllables of the living language."
[{2019-08-10} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable#Syllabification]

stem of word

description::
"the root or main part of a word, to which inflections or formative elements are added."
[{2022-01-17 retrieved} Google-dict]
===
"Root, stem, base
Taken from: Bauer, Laurie (1983:20-21): English word-formation. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
‘Root’, ‘stem’ and ‘base’ are all terms used in the literature to designate that part of a word that remains when all affixes have been removed.
A root is a form which is not further analysable, either in terms of derivational or inflectional morphology. It is that part of word-form that remains when all inflectional and derivational affixes have been removed. A root is the basic part always present in a lexeme. In the form ‘untouchables’ the root is ‘touch’, to which first the suffix ‘-able’, then the prefix ‘un-‘ and finally the suffix ‘-s’ have been added. In a compound word like ‘wheelchair’ there are two roots, ‘wheel’ and ‘chair’.
A stem is of concern only when dealing with inflectional morphology.
In the form ‘untouchables’ the stem is ‘untouchable’, although in the form ‘touched’ the stem is ‘touch’; in the form ‘wheelchairs’ the stem is ‘wheelchair’, even though the stem contains two roots.
A base is any form to which affixes of any kind can be added. This means that any root or any stem can be termed a base, but the set of bases is not exhausted by the union of the set of roots and the set of stems: a derivationally analysable form to which derivational affixes are added can only be referred to as a base. That is, ‘touchable’ can act as a base for prefixation to give ‘untouchable’, but in this process ‘touchable’ could not be referred to as a root because it is analysable in terms of derivational morphology, nor as a stem since it is not the adding of inflectional affixes which is in question."
[{2022-05-11 retrieved} ]

word.part-of-speech

description::
· traditional-grammars list parts-of-speech on MIXED criteria.
"In grammar, a part of speech or part-of-speech (abbreviated as POS or PoS, also known as word class[1] or grammatical category[2]) is a category of words (or, more generally, of lexical items) that have similar grammatical properties. Words that are assigned to the same part of speech generally display similar syntactic behavior (they play similar roles within the grammatical structure of sentences), sometimes similar morphological behavior in that they undergo inflection for similar properties and even similar semantic behavior. Commonly listed English parts of speech are noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition, conjunction, interjection, numeral, article, and determiner.
Other terms than part of speech—particularly in modern linguistic classifications, which often make more precise distinctions than the traditional scheme does—include word class, lexical class, and lexical category. Some authors restrict the term lexical category to refer only to a particular type of syntactic category; for them the term excludes those parts of speech that are considered to be function words, such as pronouns. The term form class is also used, although this has various conflicting definitions.[3] Word classes may be classified as open or closed: open classes (typically including nouns, verbs and adjectives) acquire new members constantly, while closed classes (such as pronouns and conjunctions) acquire new members infrequently, if at all.
Almost all languages have the word classes noun and verb, but beyond these two there are significant variations among different languages.[4] For example:
* Japanese has as many as three classes of adjectives, where English has one.
* Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese have a class of nominal classifiers.
* Many languages do not distinguish between adjectives and adverbs, or between adjectives and verbs (see stative verb).
Because of such variation in the number of categories and their identifying properties, analysis of parts of speech must be done for each individual language. Nevertheless, the labels for each category are assigned on the basis of universal criteria.[4]"
[{2023-05-02 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part_of_speech]
===
"A high percentage of words in a natural language are words which out of context can be assigned more than one part of speech. The percentage of these ambiguous words is typically around 30%, although it depends greatly on the language. Solving this problem is very important in many areas of natural language processing. For example in machine translation changing the part-of-speech of a word can dramatically change its translation."
[{2023-05-02 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliding_window_based_part-of-speech_tagging]

word.filler

description::
· "In linguistics, a filler, filled pause, hesitation marker or planner is a sound or word that participants in a conversation use to signal that they are pausing to think but are not finished speaking.[1][2] These are not to be confused with placeholder names, such as thingamajig, whatchamacallit, whosawhatsa and whats'isface, which refer to objects or people whose names are temporarily forgotten, irrelevant, or unknown. Fillers fall into the category of formulaic language, and different languages have different characteristic filler sounds. The term filler also has a separate use in the syntactic description of wh-movement constructions (see below)."
[{2023-06-19 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filler_(linguistics)]

"A pitch-accent language is a type of language that, when spoken, has certain syllables in words or morphemes that are prominent, as indicated by a distinct contrasting pitch (linguistic tone) rather than by loudness or length, as in some other languages like English. Pitch-accent languages also contrast with fully tonal languages like Vietnamese, Thai and Standard Chinese, in which practically every syllable can have an independent tone. Some scholars have claimed that the term "pitch accent" is not coherently defined and that pitch-accent languages are just a sub-category of tonal languages in general.[1]
Languages that have been described as pitch-accent languages include: most dialects of Serbo-Croatian, Slovene, Baltic languages, Ancient Greek, Vedic Sanskrit, Tlingit, Turkish, Japanese, Limburgish, Norwegian, Swedish of Sweden, Western Basque,[2] Yaqui,[3] certain dialects of Korean, Shanghainese,[4] and Livonian.
Pitch-accent languages tend to fall into two categories: those with a single pitch-contour (for example, high, or high–low) on the accented syllable, such as Tokyo Japanese, Western Basque, or Persian; and those in which more than one pitch-contour can occur on the accented syllable, such as Punjabi, Swedish, or Serbo-Croatian. In this latter kind, the accented syllable is also often stressed another way.
Some of the languages considered pitch-accent languages, in addition to accented words, also have accentless words (e.g., Japanese and Western Basque); in others all major words are accented (e.g., Blackfoot and Barasana).[5]
The term "pitch accent" is also used to denote a different feature, namely the use of pitch when speaking to give selective prominence (accent) to a syllable or mora within a phrase.[6]"
[{2025-04-19 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch-accent_language#English]

tone of HmnmSylb

description::
"· tones in human languages:
In human languages, tones refer to variations in pitch that can change the meaning of words. Tonal languages use these pitch changes as an integral part of their linguistic structure. Here’s an overview of tones in human languages:

### 1. **Types of Tones**
- **Level Tones:** The pitch stays at a constant level. In Mandarin Chinese, for example, there are four primary tones: high, rising, falling-rising, and falling.
- **Contour Tones:** The pitch moves up or down in a specific pattern within a syllable. Thai and Vietnamese use both level and contour tones to distinguish words.
- **Register Tones:** These involve high and low pitch levels, often seen in languages like Yoruba, which has a three-level tone system (high, mid, and low).

### 2. **Tonal Languages vs. Non-Tonal Languages**
- **Tonal Languages:** In tonal languages, tone is essential to meaning. Mandarin Chinese, Thai, Zulu, and Yoruba are all tonal languages.
- **Non-Tonal Languages:** In non-tonal languages like English, pitch may convey emotions, questions, or emphasis but does not alter the fundamental meaning of a word.

### 3. **Examples of Tonal Language Usage**
- **Mandarin Chinese:** Each syllable in Mandarin can have one of four tones, which changes its meaning. For example, "ma" with different tones can mean "mother," "hemp," "horse," or "scold."
- **Cantonese:** Has up to nine tones, including a wider range of both level and contour tones, making it a more complex tonal language.
- **Yoruba:** Uses three main tones: high, mid, and low, to differentiate between words with identical syllables.

### 4. **Why Tones Develop in Languages**
- Tones can help languages with limited syllable structure increase the number of distinct words. They are also influenced by environmental factors, linguistic evolution, and the phonetic tendencies of a language group.

### 5. **Challenges for Learners**
- Non-native speakers of tonal languages often find mastering tones challenging, as a slight pitch difference can change meanings entirely."
[{2024-11-12 retrieved} https://chatgpt.com/c/67330297-3788-8003-8fa9-752d75c6d7a1]

description::
"A naming convention is a convention (generally agreed scheme) for naming things. Conventions differ in their intents, which may include to:
* Allow useful information to be deduced from the names based on regularities. For instance, in Manhattan, streets are consecutively numbered; with east–west streets called "Streets" and north–south streets called "Avenues".
* Show relationships, and in most personal naming conventions
* Ensure that each name is unique for same scope"

name.spec-div.internal-external-use

description::
* endonym,
* exonym,

"An endonym (also known as autonym) is a common, native name for a group of people, individual person, geographical place, language or dialect, meaning that it is used inside a particular group or linguistic community to identify or designate themselves, their homeland, or their language.
An exonym (also known as xenonym) is an established, non-native name for a group of people, individual person, geographical place, language or dialect, meaning that it is used primarily outside the particular place inhabited by the group or linguistic community.[1] Exonyms exist not only for historico-geographical reasons but also in consideration of difficulties when pronouncing foreign words,[1] or from non-systematic attempts at transcribing into a different writing system.[2]
For instance, Deutschland is the endonym for the country that is also known by the exonym Germany in English, Alemania and Allemagne in Spanish and French, respectively, and Niemcy in Polish.
Some place names, used by languages which have been marginalised in areas where they historically were well established, should[opinion] still be seen as endonyms in such areas, even if some consider such place names foreign.[citation needed]"
[{2024-04-25 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endonym_and_exonym]

descriptionLong::
"The term periphrasis (from Greek períphrasis 'paraphrase, circumlocution'), in itsmost general sense, refers to the use of longer, multi-word expressions in placeof single words, or "circumlocution" (this Latin term is simply a loan translationof the Greek term). In a narrower philological context, periphrasis is one of thecanonical literary rhetorical figures (see Lausberg 1963:69),e.g. English to be hitwith Cupid's arrow 'to fall in love', or German Elbflorenz 'Florence on the Elbe =Dresden'.
For the purposes of this handbook, a still narrower, grammatical sense of theterm is relevant: Periphrasis refers to a situation in which a multi-wordexpression is used in place of a single word in an inflectional paradigm. Astandard example is the formation of comparatives in English: Many adjectiveshave an inflected comparative formed by adding the suffix -er to the base form(e.g. warm – warm-er), but other adjectives lack such a form, and comparison isconveyed by a multi-word (or phrasal) expression containing the adverb more (e.g. beautiful – more beautiful). In some intuitive sense, the phrasal expressionfulfills the same function as the inflected form with other adjectives, andlinguists have often felt the need to assimilate such "periphrastic expressions" tothe single-word forms, so that it becomes possible to say that more beautiful is the comparative form of beautiful , just as warmer is the comparative form of warm. A definition of periphrasis that reflects this reasoning is given byMatthews (1981:55): "When a form in a paradigm consists of two or more wordsit is periphrastic"."
[{2023-05-12 retrieved} https://www.academia.edu/22872072/Periphrasis]

name.common-to-languages

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-05-28}
· Do All Languages Have an Equivalent Word for “Huh”?
The use of the word "huh?" as a questioning response is virtually the same in languages all around the world.
Even if you don't speak any foreign languages, there's a good chance you already know at least one word that you can use no matter where you go: "Huh?" That's right, the seemingly nonsensical word you use to indicate that you don't understand something is basically the same sound made by people all over the world for the same reason. According to research conducted by a group from the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, the word "huh" should be seen as a remarkable linguistic invention and the first "universal word" to be studied by today's linguists. After analyzing the speech of people speaking in languages ranging from French and Spanish to the indigenous vocabulary found in Ecuador and Ghana, the researchers found that all of them used a sound very similar to "huh" to indicate a lack of understanding. Lead researcher Mark Dingemanse said the explanation for such widespread use of a word can be traced to convergent evolution. In other words, it emerges independently in different languages because it so perfectly fits its function. He compares this to the physical evolution of sharks and dolphins, which "arrived at the same body plan not because they share certain genes, but because they share an environment.”
[Read More: http://www.wisegeek.com/do-all-languages-have-an-equivalent-word-for-huh.htm?m {2020-01-16}]

description::
· identifier is a-name that denotes ONE concept.

name::
* McsEngl.ID-identifier!⇒nameId,
* McsEngl.identifier!⇒nameId,
* McsEngl.name.003-identifier!⇒nameId,
* McsEngl.name.identifier!⇒nameId,
* McsEngl.name.unique!⇒nameId,
* McsEngl.nameUnique!⇒nameId,
* McsEngl.nameId!=unique-name,
* McsEngl.unique-name!⇒nameId,

descriptionLong::
"An identifier is a name that identifies (that is, labels the identity of) either a unique object or a unique class of objects, where the "object" or class may be an idea, physical [countable] object (or class thereof), or physical [noncountable] substance (or class thereof). The abbreviation ID often refers to identity, identification (the process of identifying), or an identifier (that is, an instance of identification). An identifier may be a word, number, letter, symbol, or any combination of those.
The words, numbers, letters, or symbols may follow an encoding system (wherein letters, digits, words, or symbols stand for (represent) ideas or longer names) or they may simply be arbitrary. When an identifier follows an encoding system, it is often referred to as a code or ID code. For instance the ISO/IEC 11179 metadata registry standard defines a code as system of valid symbols that substitute for longer values in contrast to identifiers without symbolic meaning. Identifiers that do not follow any encoding scheme are often said to be arbitrary IDs; they are arbitrarily assigned and have no greater meaning. (Sometimes identifiers are called "codes" even when they are actually arbitrary, whether because the speaker believes that they have deeper meaning or simply because they are speaking casually and imprecisely.)
The unique identifier (UID) is an identifier that refers to only one instance—only one particular object in the universe. A part number is an identifier, but it is not a unique identifier—for that, a serial number is needed, to identify each instance of the part design. Thus the identifier "Model T" identifies the class (model) of automobiles that Ford's Model T comprises; whereas the unique identifier "Model T Serial Number 159,862" identifies one specific member of that class—that is, one particular Model T car, owned by one specific person.
The concepts of name and identifier are denotatively equal, and the terms are thus denotatively synonymous; but they are not always connotatively synonymous, because code names and ID numbers are often connotatively distinguished from names in the sense of traditional natural language naming. For example, both "Jamie Zawinski" and "Netscape employee number 20" are identifiers for the same specific human being; but normal English-language connotation may consider "Jamie Zawinski" a "name" and not an "identifier", whereas it considers "Netscape employee number 20" an "identifier" but not a "name". This is an emic indistinction rather than an etic one."
[{2020-07-10} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identifier]

name.systematic-013

description::
· natural-languages have no systematic-names.
===
"A systematic name is a name given in a systematic way to one unique group, organism, object or chemical substance, out of a specific population or collection. Systematic names are usually part of a nomenclature.
A semisystematic name or semitrivial name is a name that has at least one systematic part and at least one trivial part.[1][2]
Creating systematic names can be as simple as assigning a prefix or a number to each object (in which case they are a type of numbering scheme), or as complex as encoding the complete structure of the object in the name. Many systems combine some information about the named object with an extra sequence number to make it into a unique identifier.
Systematic names often co-exist with earlier common names assigned before the creation of any systematic naming system. For example, many common chemicals are still referred to by their common or trivial names, even by chemists."
[{2021-12-26 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematic_name]

argu_mebr.case

description::
· cases are-called the-members of nouns (if have more than one member) and its adjectives and articles IF the-language requires agreement with these (as eg in Greek).

"· grammatical case definition:
Grammatical case refers to the way a noun or pronoun changes its form (often through endings or accompanying words) to indicate its grammatical function or relationship to other words in a sentence. Think of it as a "role" that the noun or pronoun plays. Different cases show different roles.
Here's a breakdown with key concepts and examples, primarily focusing on how it works in concept (as English has very limited case marking compared to many other languages):
**Key Concepts**
* **Inflection:** The core concept. Case is often shown through *inflection*, meaning the noun or pronoun itself changes form. Think of the difference between "I" (subject), "me" (object), and "my" (possessive) – these are different *case forms* of the same pronoun. English nouns mostly *don't* inflect for case, except for the possessive ('s).
* **Function, not Meaning:** Case indicates the *grammatical* role, not necessarily the inherent meaning. The same noun can be in different cases depending on how it's used.
* **Agreement:** In many languages, case marking on a noun might require agreement on other words related to it, like adjectives or articles. (English has very little of this).
* **Language-Specific:** The number and types of cases vary *greatly* between languages. Some have just a few, others have dozens. English relies heavily on word order and prepositions to convey what other languages express through case.
**Common Cases (with examples in languages *other* than English, since English is limited):**
* **Nominative Case:** Usually indicates the **subject** of the verb (the one *doing* the action).
* Example (Latin): *Puer* currit. ("The *boy* runs." - *Puer* is nominative).
* Example (German): *Der Mann* liest. ("The *man* reads." - *Der Mann* is nominative).
* English equivalent relies mostly on word order: "The *boy* runs."
* **Accusative Case:** Usually indicates the **direct object** of the verb (the one *receiving* the action).
* Example (Latin): Video *puerum*. ("I see the *boy*." - *puerum* is accusative).
* Example (German): Ich sehe *den Mann*. ("I see *the man*." - *den Mann* is accusative).
* English relies mostly on word order: "I see *the boy*."
* **Genitive Case:** Usually indicates **possession, origin, or relationship**. Often translated with "of" in English.
* Example (Latin): Liber *pueri*. ("The book *of the boy* / the *boy's* book." - *pueri* is genitive).
* Example (German): Das Buch *des Mannes*. ("The book *of the man* / the *man's* book." - *des Mannes* is genitive).
* English: "The *boy's* book" (possessive 's is a remnant of the genitive) or "The book *of the boy*."
* **Dative Case:** Often indicates the **indirect object** (the recipient or beneficiary of the action), or the object of certain prepositions. Often translated with "to" or "for" in English.
* Example (Latin): Do librum *puero*. ("I give the book *to the boy*." - *puero* is dative).
* Example (German): Ich gebe *dem Mann* das Buch. ("I give *the man* the book." - *dem Mann* is dative).
* English: "I give the book *to the boy*." (preposition "to" indicates the dative function).
* **Ablative Case** (Latin, and others): Indicates **separation, movement away from, means, or instrument**. Often translated with prepositions like "from," "by," "with," or "in."
* Example (Latin): Venio *Roma*. ("I come *from Rome*." - *Roma* is ablative).
* Example (Latin): Scribo *stylo*. ("I write *with a stylus*." - *stylo* is ablative).
* English equivalent: Uses prepositions like "from," "with," etc.
* **Vocative Case:** Used for **direct address** (calling out to someone).
* Example (Latin): *Marce*, veni! ("*Marcus*, come!" - *Marce* is vocative).
* English Equivalent: *Marcus*, come! (no change in form)
* **Locative Case** (in some languages): Indicates **location** ("at," "in," "on").
* Example (Russian): в Москве (*v Moskve*) - "in Moscow" (*Moskve* is locative).
*English equivalent: uses prepositions.
* **Instrumental Case:** (in some languages, like Russian) indicates the **instrument** or **means** by which something is done.
* Example(Russian): Я пишу *ручкой* (*Ya pishu ruchkoy*) - "I write *with a pen*." (ruchkoy is instrumental)
* English equivalent: Uses the preposition "with."
**Case in English (Limited):**
* **Pronouns:** English *does* have distinct case forms for pronouns:
* **Nominative:** I, he, she, we, they, who
* **Accusative/Dative (Objective):** me, him, her, us, them, whom
* **Genitive (Possessive):** my/mine, his, her/hers, our/ours, their/theirs, whose
* **Nouns:** English nouns only have one case inflection: the possessive ('s), which is a remnant of the genitive case (e.g., "the boy's book").
* **Word Order:** English relies heavily on word order to indicate grammatical function. "The dog bit the man" has a very different meaning from "The man bit the dog," even though the nouns themselves don't change.
* **Prepositions**: English uses prepositions (to, from, with, by, in, on, etc.) to mark many of the relationships that other languages express through case endings.
**Why is this important?**
* **Understanding Other Languages:** If you learn a language with a more extensive case system (like Latin, German, Russian, Finnish, Turkish, etc.), understanding case is *crucial* to understanding the sentence structure and meaning.
* **Linguistic Analysis:** Case is a fundamental concept in linguistics, helping to describe and analyze how languages work.
* **Historical Linguistics:** Tracing the development of case systems helps us understand how languages change over time.
* Even with basic English, understanding what case *attempts* to show helps clarify the roles words play in a sentence.
In short, grammatical case is a system for marking the grammatical function of nouns and pronouns within a sentence, often through changes in their form. English has a very limited case system, relying more on word order and prepositions, but many other languages use case extensively."
[{2025-02-12 retrieved} https://gemini.google.com/app/0c64218a957392d7]

noun_mebr.aggregate

description::
"Languages such as Ancient Greek, Armenian, Assamese, most Balto-Slavic languages, Basque, most Caucasian languages, German, Icelandic, Japanese, Korean, Latin, Sanskrit, Tamil, Tibetan (one of a few tonal languages), the Turkic languages and the Uralic languages have extensive case systems, with nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and determiners all inflecting (usually by means of different suffixes) to indicate their case. The number of cases differs between languages: Persian and Esperanto have two; modern English has three but for pronouns only; German and Icelandic have four; Romanian has five; Latin, Slovenian, Russian and Turkish each have at least six; Armenian, Czech, Latvian, Lithuanian, Polish, Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian, Slovak and Ukrainian have seven; Sanskrit and Tamil have eight; Estonian has 14; Finnish has 15; Hungarian has 18 and Tsez has 64 cases."
[{2019-12-11} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_case]

description::
· main-noun is the-nominative-case of a-noun.
===
· main-argu_mebr of Hmnm_lago is a-specialNo, relationNo argu_mebr.
===
"(n) nominative, nominative case, subject case (the category of nouns serving as the grammatical subject of a verb)"
[{2022-03-25 retrieved} http://wordnetweb.princeton.edu/perl/webwn?s=nominative]
===
"In grammar, the nominative case (abbreviated nom), subjective case, straight case or upright case is one of the grammatical cases of a noun or other part of speech, which generally marks the subject of a verb or the predicate noun or predicate adjective, as opposed to its object or other verb arguments. Generally, the noun "that is doing something" is in the nominative, and the nominative is often the form listed in dictionaries."
[{2022-03-25 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nominative_case]

descriptionLong::
"Adjective comes from Latin nōmen adjectīvum,[2] a calque of Ancient Greek: ἐπίθετον ὄνομα, romanized: epítheton ónoma, lit. 'additional noun'.[3][4]
In the grammatical tradition of Latin and Greek, because adjectives were inflected for gender, number, and case like nouns (a process called declension), they were considered a type of noun.
The words that are today typically called nouns were then called substantive nouns (nōmen substantīvum).[5]
The terms noun substantive and noun adjective were formerly used in English but are now obsolete.[1]"
[{2021-12-19 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjective#Etymology]

Hmnm_adve.sentence

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-07-30}
· A **sentential adverb** (also called a **sentence adverb** or **disjunct**) is an adverb that modifies an entire sentence or clause, expressing the speaker's attitude, stance, or evaluation toward what is being said—rather than modifying a specific verb, adjective, or another adverb within the sentence.
### Key Characteristics
| Feature | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Scope** | Applies to the whole sentence, not just one word |
| **Function** | Conveys speaker comment, judgment, or frame |
| **Position** | Usually appears at the beginning, but can move |
| **Punctuation** | Often set off by commas when at the start or middle |
### Common Types
- **Evaluative:** *fortunately, unfortunately, surprisingly, oddly, luckily*
- **Modal/Probability:** *perhaps, possibly, probably, certainly, definitely*
- **Evidential:** *obviously, clearly, evidently, apparently, reportedly*
- **Speech-act/Attitudinal:** *frankly, honestly, briefly, seriously, confidentially*
### Examples
**Sentential adverb** (modifies the whole sentence):
⭢ *Fortunately*, the fire was contained quickly.
⭢ *(The speaker judges the situation as fortunate.)*
⭢ *Honestly*, I don't know what happened.
⭢ *(The speaker is commenting on the manner of their own statement.)*
⭢ The plan will, *arguably*, fail within a month.
⭢ *(The speaker signals that the following claim is debatable.)*
### Contrast with Regular Adverbs
Compare the sentential adverb with a standard **adjunct** adverb that modifies only the verb:
⭢ **Sentential:** *Clearly*, she was upset. *(It is clear to me that she was upset.)*
⭢ **Adjunct:** She spoke *clearly*. *(Her manner of speaking was clear.)*
⭢ **Sentential:** *Naturally*, he refused. *(It was natural/expected that he refused.)*
⭢ **Adjunct:** He behaves *naturally*. *(His behavior is natural in manner.)*
### Synonyms
- **Disjunct** (traditional grammar term)
- **Sentence adverb**
- **Speaker-oriented adverb**
- **Pragmatic marker** (in discourse analysis)
In short, a sentential adverb is a comment *on* the sentence rather than a modifier *within* it.

* McsElln.κλίση-ουσιαστικού!=ondoname'declension,

descriptionLong::
"In linguistics, declension is the changing of the form of a word, generally to express its syntactic function in the sentence, by way of some inflection. The inflectional change of verbs is called conjugation.
Declensions may apply to nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, and articles to indicate number (e.g., singular, dual, plural), case (e.g., nominative case, accusative case, genitive case, dative case), gender (e.g., masculine, neuter, feminine), and a number of other grammatical categories.
Declension occurs in many of the world's languages. Declension is an important aspect of language families like Quechuan (native to the Andes), Indo-European (e.g, German, Lithuanian, Latvian, Slavic, Sanskrit, Latin, Ancient and Modern Greek), Bantu (e.g., Zulu, Kikuyu), Semitic (e.g., Modern Standard Arabic), Finno-Ugric (e.g., Hungarian, Finnish, Estonian), and Turkic (e.g., Turkish).
Old English was an inflectional language, but largely abandoned inflectional changes as it evolved into Modern English. Though traditionally classified as synthetic, Modern English has moved towards an analytic language."
[{2021-06-26 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declension]

"Below is a **cross-linguistic, family-based survey** of the word **“verb”** (i.e., the *grammatical category*, not a general word meaning “action”), with **native script + standard romanization**.
Where relevant, I note whether the term is **native** or a **learned borrowing** (often from Latin *verbum*).
---
## Indo-European
### Romance (from Latin *verbum*)

| Latin | verbum | verbum | Source term |
| French | verbe | verbe | Borrowed |
| Spanish | verbo | verbo | Borrowed |
| Italian | verbo | verbo | Borrowed |
| Portuguese | verbo | verbo | Borrowed |
| Romanian | verb | verb | Borrowed |
### Germanic
| English | verb | verb | Borrowed |
| German | Verb | Verb | Borrowed |
| Dutch | werkwoord | werkwoord | Native compound |
| Swedish | verb | verb | Borrowed |
| Icelandic | sögn | sögn | Native |
### Slavic

| Bulgarian | глагол | glagol | Native |
### Hellenic

### Observations (Linguistically Relevant)
* **Latin *verbum*** dominates European metalanguage.
* **Semitic languages** use derivations of the *f-ʿ-l* (“do”) root.
* Many languages use **semantic paraphrases**:
*“action-word”*, *“doing-word”*, *“time-word”*.
* Learned vs native terminology often reflects **grammatical tradition vs vernacular grammar**.

etymology::
"The word "verb" comes from Latin **verbum**, which meant "word." This Latin term is itself derived from the Proto-Indo-European root ***werh₁-**, meaning "to speak" or "to say."
The shift from meaning simply "word" to specifically meaning "action word" or "verb" happened through Latin grammar terminology. Roman grammarians used *verbum* in the specific sense of the part of speech that expresses action or state of being, to distinguish it from *nomen* (noun). This specialized grammatical meaning was then borrowed into Old French as *verbe*, and from there into Middle English around the 14th century.
Interestingly, the original broader meaning of "word" is preserved in expressions like "the Word of God" (where *verbum* referred to divine speech or logos), and in words like "verbal," which can mean "relating to words" more generally, not just verbs specifically.
The same PIE root also gave us English words like "word" itself (through Germanic), showing the deep linguistic connection between these terms for speech and language across Indo-European languages."
[{2026-01-03 retrieved} https://claude.ai/chat/3f54858c-877c-481f-afc2-55665cfe9d27]

verb_mebr.participle

description::
"In linguistics, a participle (ptcp) (from Latin participium a "sharing, partaking") is a nonfinite verb form that has some of the characteristics and functions of both verbs and adjectives.[1] More narrowly, participle has been defined as "a word derived from a verb and used as an adjective, as in a laughing face".[2]
“Participle” is a traditional grammatical term from Greek and Latin that is widely used for corresponding verb forms in European languages and analogous forms in Sanskrit and Arabic grammar.
Cross-linguistically, participles may have a range of functions apart from adjectival modification. In European and Indian languages, the past participle is used to form the passive voice. In English, participles are also associated with periphrastic verb forms (continuous and perfect) and are widely used in adverbial clauses. In non-Indo-European languages, ‘participle’ has been applied to forms that are alternatively regarded as converbs (see Sireniki Eskimo below), gerunds, gerundives, transgressives, and nominalised verbs in complement clauses. As a result, ‘participles’ have come to be associated with a broad variety of syntactic constructions."
[{2022-04-18 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Participle]

verb_mebr.voice.active

description::
· active-look--verb_mebr is a-verb NOT in relation to what DENOTES but in relation to its appearance.
· they are-called 'active' because they are-used to express that the-subject of action-verbs is the-doer of the-action, BUT they are-used to express and other verbs such as function and relation ones.
===
"In grammar, the voice of a verb describes the relationship between the action (or state) that the verb expresses and the participants identified by its arguments (subject, object, etc.). When the subject is the agent or doer of the action, the verb is in the active voice. When the subject is the patient, target or undergoer of the action, the verb is said to be in the passive voice. Voice is sometimes called diathesis.[1]"
[{2019-08-16} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_(grammar)]

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-02-13}
"· verb creation in world languages:
Based on the search results, I can provide detailed information about verb creation processes in world languages. The available information focuses heavily on **denominal verb formation** (creating verbs from nouns) and **verb inflection acquisition**, with excellent detailed data on specific languages like Etulo, Portuguese, and English. However, the search results do not contain a comprehensive global survey of verb creation across all language families.
Here is a synthesis of the major verb-creation strategies documented in the provided sources:
## 1. Denominal and Deadjectival Verb Formation (Nouns/Adjectives → Verbs)
The most extensively documented process in your sources is the creation of verbs from other parts of speech, particularly nouns and adjectives. This is identified as the **major source of new verbs** in many languages .
**Three primary morphological processes** are identified in English and Portuguese :
| Process | Definition | English Examples | Portuguese Examples |
| **Suffixation** | Adding a verb-forming suffix | `cod` → `codify`; `fragile` → `fragilize` | `plan` → `planificar` (to plan) |
| **Conversion (Zero-derivation)** | Using a word as a verb without adding an affix | `water` (n) → `water` (v); `dry` (adj) → `dry` (v) | `jogo` (game) → `jogar` (to play) |
| **Parasynthesis** | Adding both a prefix and a suffix simultaneously; the word does not exist without both | `globe` → `en**globe**` (cannot say "globe" as verb or "englobe" without prefix?); `rich` → `en**rich**` | `buraco` (hole) → `es**buracar**` (to make a hole) |
**Key Insight:** In parasynthesis, the verb is formed by attaching both a prefix and a suffix at the same time. You cannot remove one and keep a valid verb (e.g., in Portuguese, *esburacar* exists, but *buracar* does not) .
## 2. Derivation from Verbs (Verb → Verb)
Verbs can also be formed from existing verbs, often to **change the valency** (number of arguments) or aspect of the action .
* **Causative Formation**: Changing the verb to indicate that the subject causes something to happen (e.g., *to fall* → *to fell* meaning "to cause to fall"). This is a major typological category .
* **Aspectual and Manner Modification**: Adding morphology to change how the action occurs (e.g., iterative, habitual) .
## 3. Affixation, Compounding, and Reduplication (Case Study: Etulo)
A highly detailed account of verb-related morphology is provided for **Etulo**, an Idomoid language of Nigeria. This serves as an excellent example of how a single language utilizes multiple processes .
* **Infinitive Formation**: Formed by adding a **low-tone vowel prefix (`ò-`)** to the bare verb root (e.g., `gíé` "eat" → `ògíé` "to eat") .
* **Gerundive Formation**: Created through a combination of **three simultaneous processes**: (1) prefix `ò-`, (2) **reduplication** of the verb root, and (3) **tonal modification** (e.g., `ʃí` "sing" → `ò-ʃǐ-ʃǐ` "singing") .
* **Agentive Nouns**: Often formed by combining the gerundive form with the generic noun `ǹgísɛ̀` (person), though some lexicalized forms exist without it (e.g., `òtsètsê` "teacher") .
## 4. Inflectional Morphology (Verb Forms)
While derivation *creates new words*, inflection *modifies existing verbs* for grammar. Your results include a major study on how children acquire this in **Polish and Finnish**. These languages have highly complex systems where verbs inflect for **person, number, and tense** .
* Children acquire these systems not just by memorization, but by using **phonological analogy** (grouping verbs that sound similar) and responding to **token frequency** .
## 5. Compounding and Other Lexical Processes
* **Compounding**: Combining two free morphemes to create a new verb or deverbal noun (e.g., English `head bracelet`; Mandarin Chinese compounds mentioned in typological overviews) .
* **Backformation/Coinage**: Creating a verb by removing an affix from an existing noun (e.g., `conversation` → `conversate`; `autoclave` (n) → `autoclave` (v)) .
## Summary of Typological Patterns
The search results confirm that languages differ dramatically in how freely they create verbs :
* **Germanic Languages (e.g., English)**: Highly productive **conversion** (zero-derivation) is very common.
* **Romance Languages (e.g., Portuguese, French)**: Reliance on **suffixation** and **parasynthesis**.
* **Isolating/Analytic Languages (e.g., Etulo)**: Reliance on **isolated morphemes/particles** and **reduplication** rather than complex affix chains .
**Gap in results:** The search results focused heavily on English, Portuguese, and Etulo. While Japanese is briefly mentioned in relation to nominalization and stative predicates, no detailed data on Japanese verb creation mechanics was provided in the accessible text . Additionally, one result regarding verb priming in bilinguals was focused on psychology/cognition, not morphological typology .
If you would like me to look for specific information regarding verb creation in a specific language family not covered here (such as Semitic root-pattern verbs, Bantu extension morphology, or East Asian languages), please let me know."

"· verb creation in world languages:
Verb creation (how languages **form new verbs**) varies widely across the world, but most strategies fall into a few recurring **typological patterns**. Below is a cross-linguistic overview with examples from different language families.
---
## 1. **Derivation with Affixes**
Adding prefixes, suffixes, or infixes to a root is the **most common** method.
![Image](https://storage.googleapis.com/static.prod.fiveable.me/search-images%2F%22Inflectional_vs_derivational_morphology_in_linguistics%3A_examples_differences_and_word_formation_processes%22-300px-Independently_morphology_tree.png)
![Image](https://2.bp.blogspot.com/-_b0GIyqzylw/UREcgmtrfVI/AAAAAAAAA1M/n2gAnLEDXhY/s1600/common%2Broots.PNG)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/337062697/figure/tbl2/AS%3A822289004261379%401573060384682/Verbalizers-Verb-derivational-affixes.png)
### Examples
* **English (Germanic)**
* *modern* → *modern-ize*
* *nation* → *nation-al-ize*
* **Spanish (Romance)**
* *blanco* (white) → *blanqu-ear* (to whiten)
* **Turkish (Turkic)**
* *temiz* (clean) → *temiz-le-mek* (to clean)
* **Swahili (Bantu)**
* *-soma* (read) → *-somesha* (cause to read)
➡️ Often encodes **causative, reflexive, reciprocal, or aspectual** meaning.
---
## 2. **Conversion (Zero Derivation)**
A word changes category **without any visible marking**.
![Image](https://lhncbc.nlm.nih.gov/LSG/Projects/lvg/current/docs/designDoc/UDF/derivations/zeroD.jpg)
![Image](https://imgv2-1-f.scribdassets.com/img/document/464860094/original/54bad60a3b/1?v=1)
![Image](https://www.grammar-monster.com/images/most-common-English-verbs.webp)
### Examples
* **English**
* *to email*, *to bottle*, *to Google*
* **Mandarin Chinese**
* *爱* (*ài*) = “love” (noun or verb, context decides)
➡️ Common in **analytic languages** with minimal morphology.
---
## 3. **Light Verb Constructions**
A noun combines with a **semantically light verb** (“do”, “make”, “give”).
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/349569406/figure/tbl1/AS%3A994741038624782%401614176153996/examples-of-light-verb-constructions.png)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237328214/figure/tbl1/AS%3A669389456171013%401536606291596/Classification-of-Persian-Light-Verbs.png)
![Image](https://figures.semanticscholar.org/feb1f43d6cb789f633406434b99ad8861706d73c/3-Figure1-1.png)
### Examples
* **Persian**
* *kar kardan* (work do) = “to work”
* **Hindi**
* *nirṇay lenā* (decision take) = “to decide”
* **Japanese**
* *勉強する* (*benkyō suru*) = “to study”
➡️ Productive, flexible, and common in **Indo-Iranian & East Asian** languages.
---
## 4. **Compounding**
Two or more roots combine into a new verb.
![Image](https://assets.ltkcontent.com/images/33305/compound-verb-examples_27c5571306.jpg)
![Image](https://xyz.tingroom.com/file/upload//202302/03/100536491.png)
![Image](https://khanjischool.com/uploads/images/c/1/l/sqf-compound-verbs-in-chinese-grammar-examples-illustration.jpg)
### Examples
* **German**
* *kennenlernen* (“know+learn” = meet)
* **Chinese**
* *学习* (*xuéxí*) = “study” (learn+practice)
* **Yoruba**
* Serial verb combinations expressing complex actions
➡️ Often expresses **manner + action** or **cause + result**.
---
## 5. **Causative Formation**
Languages explicitly mark “make/let someone do X”.
![Image](https://esllibrary.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/ckeditor/pictures/215/content_103_Causative-Verbs-Have-Let-Make.png)
![Image](https://i.pinimg.com/736x/63/ae/1f/63ae1ff51b8a02689d687f2a43d3089e.jpg)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263545324/figure/tbl1/AS%3A392430005309444%401470574012632/List-of-all-verbal-patterns-in-Arabic-Information-on-the-transliteration-system-used.png)
### Examples
* **Japanese**
* *食べる* (*taberu*, eat) → *食べさせる* (*tabesaseru*, make eat)
* **Hebrew**
* Root *k-t-b* (write) → causative pattern *hixtiv* (dictate)
* **Quechua**
* Suffix *-chi* adds causation
---
## 6. **Reduplication**
Repeating all or part of a root to create or modify a verb.
![Image](https://i.pinimg.com/736x/95/1c/b5/951cb5d51cd1e422c16dbdba3bb680f6.jpg)
![Image](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f0/Austroneske_jazyky.jpg)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/365958150/figure/tbl1/AS%3A11431281104268664%401669989577564/The-full-reduplication-of-English-and-Indonesian-Language.png)
### Examples
* **Indonesian**
* *jalan* (walk) → *jalan-jalan* (stroll around)
* **Tagalog**
* Aspect and intensity via reduplication
* **African & Pacific languages**
* Iteration, intensity, or habitual meaning
---
## 7. **Root-and-Pattern Systems**
Verbs are created by inserting roots into **vowel/consonant patterns**.
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228963297/figure/fig1/AS%3A669415066583050%401536612397428/Root-pattern-morphology-3rd-person-singular-masculine-sound-perfect-active-form-I-verb.png)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272488329/figure/tbl1/AS%3A669552899788805%401536645259233/The-ten-derived-verb-forms-in-Arabic.png)
![Image](https://lilmod-aleph-beth.fr/IMG/CONJUGAISON/Futur/Groupe-POUAL-10-verbes-conjugues-au-Future.jpg)
### Examples
* **Arabic**
* Root *k-t-b* → *kataba* (write), *kattaba* (cause to write)
* **Hebrew**
* Same root yields passive, reflexive, causative verbs
➡️ Highly systematic, meaning encoded structurally.
---
## 8. **Incorporation**
Objects or modifiers are absorbed into the verb.
![Image](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs11049-021-09511-4/MediaObjects/11049_2021_9511_Figae_HTML.png)
![Image](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b5/English_Syntax_Tree_Example.png)
![Image](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Mohawk_Noun_Incorporation_Syntax_Tree.png/250px-Mohawk_Noun_Incorporation_Syntax_Tree.png)
### Examples
* **Mohawk**
* “I-fish-eat” = “I eat fish”
* **Inuktitut**
* Whole sentences expressed as a single verb
➡️ Common in **polysynthetic languages**.
---
## Typological Summary
| Language Type | Common Verb Creation |
| Analytic | Conversion, light verbs |
| Agglutinative | Affix stacking |
| Fusional | Stem alternations |
| Polysynthetic | Incorporation |
| Root-pattern | Morphological templates |
---
## Big Picture Insight
⭢ All languages balance **expressiveness vs. economy**:
* Some create many verbs morphologically
* Others rely on syntax and context
* But **every language has productive ways to “verb” new meanings**
If you want, I can:
* Compare **English vs Greek verb formation**
* Analyze **verb creation in programming languages vs natural languages**
* Go deeper into **historical evolution of verbs**
* Show how **new verbs enter modern languages (e.g., tech slang)**"

"· Show how new verbs enter modern languages:
Here’s a **clear, modern linguistics view** of **how brand-new verbs enter living languages today**, focusing on *mechanisms, social forces, and real-time change*.
---
## 1. Nouns → Verbs (Verbification / Conversion)
This is currently the **fastest and most productive** pathway, especially in English and other analytic languages.
![Image](https://josecarilloforum.com/imgs/nerb-conversion-samples_chart-1B1.png)
![Image](https://cdn.innovativelanguage.com/sns/em/blog/19/10_internet_slang/Computer_Words/English_technology.png)
![Image](https://media.spokesman.com/photos/2009/09/06/horsey-google.jpg)
### How it works
A noun is reinterpreted as an action **without morphology**.
### Examples
* *to Google*
* *to text*
* *to friend / unfriend*
* *to Zoom*
* *to DM*
### Why it dominates today
* Minimal effort
* No agreement or conjugation barriers
* Works instantly in speech
➡️ **Insight:** English has become a *verb-first innovation language*.
---
## 2. Borrowing + Native Verb Morphology
Languages with richer morphology **adapt loanwords** into existing verb systems.
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/345036255/figure/tbl4/AS%3A952642360602625%401604139046761/frequent-loan-verbs-in-the-corpus12.png)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/330702541/figure/tbl3/AS%3A720328259039233%401548751048573/Examples-of-indirect-word-level-borrowing.png)
![Image](https://images.twinkl.co.uk/tw1n/image/private/t_630/u/ux/base-verbs-image-english-grammar-teaching-wiki_ver_1.png)
### Patterns
* Borrow noun → add verb suffix
* Borrow stem → adapt phonology
### Examples
* Spanish: *googlear*, *tuitear*
* Greek: *σκανάρω* (scan), *κατεβάζω* (download)
* Japanese: *ダウンロードする* (download + do)
➡️ Borrowing **respects the internal grammar** of the language.
---
## 3. Light Verb Constructions (Global Strategy)
Instead of inventing a new verb, languages **wrap a noun in an existing verb**.
![Image](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/cover/isbn/9783110747997/product)
![Image](https://www.sprachcaffe.com/fileadmin/_processed_/d/a/csm_Do_and_Does_in_English___Simple_Present_Tense_Questions___Learn_English_DO_vs._DOES_13013e11e1.png)
![Image](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/2aa2f20f-750c-4bf6-aa5e-7cd26f26015b_1.png)
### Common light verbs
* do
* make
* take
* give
### Examples
* *make a call*
* *do a download*
* Spanish: *hacer clic*
* Hindi: *message karna*
➡️ This allows **instant adoption without restructuring grammar**.
---
## 4. Branding → Verbization (Corporate Influence)
Modern verbs increasingly originate from **brands**, a historically new phenomenon.
![Image](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/ce76ad_5f4bfae5d3fc413fa7d08720505ad574~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_2048%2Ch_1290%2Cal_c/ce76ad_5f4bfae5d3fc413fa7d08720505ad574~mv2.jpg)
![Image](https://imgv2-2-f.scribdassets.com/img/document/482880475/original/d8028260c0/1?v=1)
![Image](https://fastercapital.com/i/Language-global-leadership-The-Power-of-Language-in-Global-Entrepreneurship--The-Influence-of-Language-on-Global-Branding.webp)
### Examples
* *to Uber*
* *to Venmo*
* *to Photoshop*
* *to Airbnb*
### Linguistic rule
⭢ If a brand becomes a **default action**, it becomes a verb.
Companies often resist this (loss of trademark control), but **language wins**.
---
## 5. Semantic Narrowing → Expansion
Existing verbs gain **new digital meanings**.
![Image](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/app/uploads/sites/1310/2023/06/14.x-widening-arrive.png)
![Image](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/785fce73-71ac-4927-ad70-58bdff3f2883/cogs13141-fig-0001-m.png)
![Image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Matoseb/Scrollbars/master/rsrc/screenshot_01.jpg)
### Examples
* *scroll* (roll → digital motion)
* *post* (mail → online publish)
* *stream* (water → data flow)
* *follow* (physical → social media)
➡️ Metaphor drives verb innovation more than invention.
---
## 6. Slang → Mainstream → Grammar
Many verbs start as **youth slang**, then stabilize.
![Image](https://miro.medium.com/v2/da%3Atrue/resize%3Afit%3A1200/0%2ATLz71RNoY5N7TvE7)
![Image](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/658c78b80738c0694e2ea1ba/6645cf7074ae7aba7327623c_1.png)
![Image](https://i.pinimg.com/1200x/1d/51/de/1d51de0209e224201d0e3bce1a7af40c.jpg)
### Examples
* *ghost* (sudden disappearance)
* *flex* (show off)
* *clap back* (retaliate verbally)
* *ship* (support a relationship)
### Survival filter
* High frequency
* Broad applicability
* Social prestige
Most slang verbs **die fast**; a few become permanent.
---
## 7. Productivity Rules: Why Some Verbs Stick
A new verb survives if it:
1. Fits phonology
2. Conjugates easily
3. Encodes a **repeatable action**
4. Solves a lexical gap
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/249745075/figure/tbl8/AS%3A670031776063488%401536759432011/Productive-likely-productive-and-unproductive-verbs-in-stage-3.png)
![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%218MmW%21%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd6c9722d-caf0-49f7-85cd-a680b17fd701_1564x975.png)
![Image](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/I/51Lyd-rGSIL._AC_UF894%2C1000_QL80_.jpg)
### Example contrast
* *to fax* → obsolete
* *to text* → permanent
* *to tweet* → unstable (platform-dependent)
➡️ Technology lifespan affects verb survival.
---
## 8. Grammaticalization Begins Immediately
Some modern verbs are **already turning grammatical**.
![Image](https://i.sstatic.net/T23UD.png)
![Image](https://www.oysterenglish.com/images/xbe-going-to.png.pagespeed.ic.B2TYokIe91.png)
![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21RoDj%21%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F914ebe37-0a87-47bb-a180-723934885d55_1134x756.png)
### Early signals
* Reduced pronunciation
* Fixed position
* Abstract meaning
Example:
* *I’m gonna* → future marker
* *lemme* ← *let me*
This shows **language change in real time**.
---
## 9. Cross-Linguistic Contrast (Modern Snapshot)
| Language Type | Preferred Strategy |
| English | Zero derivation |
| Romance | Suffixation |
| Slavic | Prefix/aspect marking |
| Japanese | Noun + する |
| Arabic | Root-pattern adaptation |
➡️ Global tech verbs adapt differently, but **enter everywhere**.
---
## 10. Big Takeaway
⭢ **Modern verb creation is faster, flatter, and socially driven.**
* Tech accelerates innovation
* Branding influences grammar
* Youth slang seeds change
* Grammar absorbs verbs within decades—not centuries
Languages today are evolving **faster than ever**, but using **the same ancient mechanisms**.
---
If you want next, we can:
* Track **one verb across 5 languages**
* Predict **which current verbs will survive**
* Compare **digital vs pre-industrial verb creation**
* Connect this to **programming language design**
Just say the word."
[{2026-02-13 retrieved} https://chatgpt.com/c/698eeac5-a7c8-8387-84dd-f31055405b70]

name::
* McsEngl.verb'creating,

evoluting of verb

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2026-02-13}
"Below is a **deep historical dive** into how verbs evolve over time, focusing on **mechanisms, timelines, and recurring cross-linguistic patterns** rather than just surface forms.
---
## 1. From Concrete Actions → Abstract Processes
Early verbs overwhelmingly described **physical, observable actions**. Over time, they expand metaphorically.
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263356263/figure/fig2/AS%3A296498865688578%401447702246600/Abstract-versus-Whole-Concrete-verbs-comparison-Panel-A-Grand-averaged-ERPs-for.png)
![Image](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/785fce73-71ac-4927-ad70-58bdff3f2883/cogs13141-fig-0001-m.png)
![Image](https://www.glossa-journal.org/article/id/5231/file/64040/)
### Typical Path
**physical action → social action → mental / abstract state**
**Examples**
* *grasp* → understand
* *see* → know (*“I see your point”*)
* *stand* → tolerate (*“I can’t stand this”*)
🔎 **Why this happens**
Human cognition is grounded in the body. Abstract thought piggybacks on physical experience.
---
## 2. Lexical Verbs → Grammatical Verbs (Grammaticalization)
One of the most important processes in verb evolution.
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272040897/figure/fig2/AS%3A391968686395394%401470464025880/Degree-of-grammaticalization-of-directional-verbs-faan-1-and-maai-4.png)
![Image](https://www.grammar-monster.com/glossary/pics/auxilliary_verbs.webp)
![Image](https://english.eagetutor.com/images/FUTURE-TENSES-OVERVIEW.png)
### Common Evolution Chains
| Original Meaning | New Function |
| ---------------- | ----------------------- |
| want | future tense |
| go | future / aspect |
| have | perfect tense |
| give | causative / benefactive |
### Examples
* *I am going to eat* → future marker
* French *avoir* (“have”) → perfect auxiliary
* Mandarin *给* (*give*) → causative marker
➡️ **Key insight**: verbs lose lexical meaning but gain **grammatical power**.
---
## 3. Erosion: Sound Loss & Irregularity
Frequent verbs erode phonetically and become **irregular**.
![Image](https://www.eslprintables.com/previews/665373_1-Irregular_verbs_sound_patterns_easy_to_memorize_2_pages_only_.jpg)
![Image](https://0.academia-photos.com/attachment_thumbnails/55594547/mini_magick20190114-19491-aug1ag.png?1547474490=)
![Image](https://www.teflcourse.net/images/infogrammars/big/fbe9e3d4413402318be63455c367bc37.jpg)
### Pattern
* High frequency → sound reduction → irregular forms
**English**
* *helped* (regular)
* *went* (from *wend*)
* *was / were* (multiple historical mergers)
**Cross-linguistic rule**
⭢ The **more common a verb**, the **less regular** it becomes.
This is why verbs like *be*, *go*, *do*, *have* are irregular worldwide.
---
## 4. Aspect Before Tense (Universals of Verb Evolution)
Historically, **aspect** precedes **tense**.
![Image](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/2473/3068/files/BLOG5PIC_1156x1156.png?v=1640281950)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326043976/figure/tbl1/AS%3A669068470259730%401536529762992/Perfective-and-imperfective-verb-forms.png)
![Image](https://fiveable.me/_next/image?q=75\&url=https%3A%2F%2Fstorage.googleapis.com%2Fstatic.prod.fiveable.me%2Fsearch-images%252F%2522Old_English_verb_tenses_chart_present_past_future_moods_aspects_study_guide_illustration%2522-jce2v6cnqdgefzggvwnu.jpe%2523fixme.jpg\&w=3840)
### Early Distinctions
* completed vs ongoing
* habitual vs punctual
* repeated vs single event
Only later do languages grammaticalize **time reference** (past/future).
**Evidence**
* Ancient Indo-European
* Semitic
* Mayan languages
➡️ Humans care first about **how** an action happens, not *when*.
---
## 5. Verb Serialization → Prepositions → Case Markers
Many verbs shrink into grammatical markers.
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/329548406/figure/fig1/AS%3A11431281215326323%401704162442940/Categories-of-serial-verb-construction.png)
![Image](https://imgv2-1-f.scribdassets.com/img/document/509120198/original/a70b58b852/1?v=1)
![Image](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f9/ECM_trees_1.png)
### Example Path
**verb → directional verb → preposition → case ending**
* “go inside” → “inside” → locative case
* “give to” → dative marker
Seen in:
* Niger-Congo
* Sino-Tibetan
* Indo-European (historically)
---
## 6. Roots vs Stems: Why Some Languages Preserve Structure
Some languages preserve ancient **root systems**, others erode them.
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339639947/figure/fig1/AS%3A864824032497664%401583201525209/Root-Pattern-Morphology-Process.png)
![Image](https://cdn.britannica.com/09/128209-050-5D80A96D/Migration-languages-Afro-Asiatic-Middle-Eastern-Urheimat.jpg)
![Image](https://cdn.britannica.com/87/1987-050-D586063D/Examples-noun-inflection-Sanskrit-Hittite-Greek-languages.jpg)
### Two Strategies
**Root-based**
* Meaning in consonantal skeleton
* Patterns encode voice/aspect/causation
**Stem-based**
* Entire word reshaped by sound change
* Morphology becomes opaque
➡️ Both descend from earlier **transparent systems**.
---
## 7. Verb Creation During Language Contact
Contact accelerates verb evolution.
![Image](https://fiveable.me/_next/image?q=75\&url=https%3A%2F%2Fstorage.googleapis.com%2Fstatic.prod.fiveable.me%2Fsearch-images%252F%2522Language_contact_and_linguistic_borrowing_examples_bilingualism_cultural_exchange_influence_on_vocabulary_and_dialects%2522-Loanword_classification_tree_3.gif\&w=3840)
![Image](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/345036255/figure/tbl4/AS%3A952642360602625%401604139046761/frequent-loan-verbs-in-the-corpus12.png)
![Image](https://publish.iupress.indiana.edu/api/proxy/ingestion_sources/ae17302f-80d0-4ae9-af0f-1772a6036a89)
### Borrowing Strategies
* Add native verb suffix
* Use light verb (“do X”)
* Convert noun → verb
**Examples**
* *download-ear* (Spanish)
* *hacer clic* (“do click”)
* *to Google*
---
## 8. Cycles in Verb Systems (Renewal)
Languages repeatedly **lose** and **rebuild** verb categories.
![Image](https://64.media.tumblr.com/b945709611b46e82144041d10998e071/tumblr_myi78lg6F61rnvzfwo1_1280.jpg)
![Image](https://fiveable.me/_next/image?q=75\&url=https%3A%2F%2Fstorage.googleapis.com%2Fstatic.prod.fiveable.me%2Fsearch-images%252F%2522Main_tenses_in_English%253A_past_present_future_with_examples_and_usage_in_grammar%2522-bBM3R.jpg\&w=3840)
![Image](https://a.storyblok.com/f/236180/7cc8e7611b/tiempos-verbales-en-ingles-min-1024x611.jpg)
### Typical Cycle
1. Full verb (“want”)
2. Auxiliary
3. Affix
4. Erosion
5. Replacement by new verb
This cycle can take **500–2000 years**.
---
## 9. Why Verbs Change Faster Than Nouns
| Feature | Verbs | Nouns |
| Frequency | Very high | Lower |
| Grammar load | Heavy | Light |
| Sound erosion | Fast | Slower |
| Irregularity | Common | Rare |
➡️ Verbs sit at the **interface of meaning and grammar**, making them unstable.
---
## 10. Big Historical Insight
⭢ **Verbs are where language turns thought into structure.**
They evolve:
* from action → abstraction
* from words → grammar
* from clarity → efficiency
This is why verb systems tell us **more about a language’s history** than almost anything else.
---
If you want, next we can:
* Trace **English verbs from Proto-Indo-European**
* Compare **Greek vs Latin verb evolution**
* Analyze **why programming languages imitate natural verb systems**
* Explore **how AI and tech slang are reshaping verbs today**
Just tell me which direction you want to go."
[{2026-02-13 retrieved} https://chatgpt.com/c/698eeac5-a7c8-8387-84dd-f31055405b70]

descriptionLong::
"The term equative (or equational) is used in linguistics to refer to constructions where two entities are equated with each other. For example, the sentence Susan is our president, equates two entities "Susan" and "our president". In English, equatives are typically expressed using a copular verb such as "be", although this is not the only use of this verb. Equatives can be contrasted with predicative constructions where one entity is identified as a member of a set, such as Susan is a president. This view has been contrasted by Otto Jespersen in the first part of the XX century and by Giuseppe Longobardi and Andrea Moro in the second. In particular, Andrea Moro in 1988 proved that either DP must be non referential in the sense of Geach (1962) by exploiting arguments based on binding theory. The idea is that when a DP plays the role of predicate it enlarges its binding domain: for example, in John met his cook the pronoun can refer to the subject John but in John is his cook it cannot. The key-step was to admit that the DP following the copula can be referential whereas the one preceding must not, in other words the key-step was to admit that there can be inverse copular sentences, namely those where the subject, which is referential, follows the predicate. For a discussion starting from Moro's data see Heycock (2012). For a historical view of the development of the analysis of the copula see Moro
Different world languages approach equatives in different ways. The major difference between languages is whether or not they use a copular verb or a non-verbal element (e.g. demonstrative pronoun) to equate the two expressions.
The term equative is also sometimes applied to comparative-like constructions in which the degrees compared are identical rather than distinct: e.g., John is as stupid as he is blonde; some languages have a separate equative case."
[{2021-10-10 retrieved} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equative]

descriptionLong::
"Multi-word verbs are verbs that consist of more than one word.[1] This term may cover both periphrasis as in combinations involving modal or semi-modal auxiliaries with an additional verbal or other lexeme, e.g. had better, used to, be going to, ought to, phrasal verbs, as in combinations of verbs and particles,[2] and compound verbs as in light-verb constructions, e.g. take a shower, have a meal."

verb.modal|auxiliary

description::
× Mcsh-creation: {2025-10-15}
· special verbs that in SOME languages have special syntax.

=== can:
· _sntxEngl: I can write. special.
· _sntxElln: μπορώ να-γράψε. normal.

In linguistics, modals are expressions broadly associated with notions of possibility and necessity. Modals have a wide variety of interpretations which depend not only upon the particular modal used, but also upon where the modal occurs in a sentence, the meaning of the sentence independent of the modal, the conversational context, and a variety of other factors. For example, the interpretation of an English sentence containing the modal 'must' can be that of a statement of inference or knowledge (roughly, epistemic) or a statement of how something ought to be (roughly, deontic). The following pair of examples illustrate the interpretative difference:
(1) John didn't show up for work. He must be sick.
(2) John didn't show up for work. He must be fired.
[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_modality]

Verbs that "help" other verbs to express necessity, possibility and willingness are called auxiliary verbs. Auxiliary verbs are often used to modify verbs or adjectives. A noun cannot immediately follow them. They are negated by bu4.
Auxiliary verbs include the following kinds:
1. Those expressing capability:
2. Those expressing possibility:
3. Those expressing necessity by reason:
4. Those expressing obligation:
5. Those expressing willingness:

description::
"The term ‘light verb’ (LV), coined by Jespersen (1954), refers to verbs such as have and give in complex predicate constructions like have a bath and give a push, where the main semantic content is provided not by the verb, but by the action nominal, for example bath and push. In a general sense, the light verb construction (LVC) have a bath roughly means bathe. From a typological perspective, LVCs have close historical association with their independent verb counterparts (see Butt 2003; Butt and Lahiri 2002, among others)."
[{2021-11-30 retrieved} https://www.soas.ac.uk/linguistics/research/workingpapers/volume-18/file115990.pdf]

description::
· conjunction-of-Hmnm_lago is a-term that denotes a-semu_conj (a-directed-timeless-relation).
===
"Conjunctions are **words (or affixes) that connect units of language**—words, phrases, clauses, or sentences. Every known human language has some way to express conjunction-like relationships, but **how they do it varies widely**.
Below is a **cross-linguistic overview** of conjunctions and how different languages handle them.
---
## 1. Main types of conjunctions (near-universal functions)
Most languages express these **core logical relations**, even if they don’t always use standalone words.
| Function | Meaning | English |
| **Coordination** | add / link | and |
| **Alternative** | choice | or |
| **Contrast** | opposition | but |
| **Subordination** | dependency | because, if, that |
| **Temporal** | time | when, while |
| **Conditional** | condition | if |
| **Causal** | reason | because |
| **Purpose** | goal | so that |
---
## 2. European languages (Indo-European pattern)
Most European languages use **free-standing conjunction words**.
| Language | “and” | “or” | “but” |
| English | and | or | but |
| French | et | ou | mais |
| German | und | oder | aber |
| Spanish | y | o | pero |
| Greek | και | ή | αλλά |
🔹 Characteristics:
* Clear separation between **coordinating** and **subordinating** conjunctions
* Subordinate clauses often marked by a **specific word + verb form**
---
## 3. Languages with particles instead of words
Some languages use **particles** that attach loosely to clauses rather than acting like independent words.
### Japanese
* **と (to)** – and (lists)
* **や (ya)** – and/or (non-exhaustive)
* **が (ga)** – but
* **から (kara)** – because
⭢ 雨が降った**から**行かなかった
⭢ “Because it rained, I didn’t go.”
### Korean
* **-고 (-go)** – and (verb-linking)
* **하지만 (hajiman)** – but
* **그래서 (geuraeseo)** – so / therefore
🔹 Often **verb-final**, conjunctions link **clauses**, not words.
---
## 4. Languages that use verb morphology instead
Some languages **don’t need conjunction words at all**.
### Turkic languages (e.g., Turkish)
Instead of “because / when / if”, they often use **verbal suffixes**:
* **-ince** → when
* **-diği için** → because
* **-se** → if
⭢ Geldiğimde seni gördüm
⭢ “When I came, I saw you.”
🔹 The verb itself carries the conjunction meaning.
---
## 5. Parataxis: no conjunctions required
Some languages rely heavily on **parataxis**—placing clauses next to each other and letting context do the work.
### Classical Chinese
⭢ 雨下，路滑
⭢ “Rain falls, road slippery”
⭢ → “Because it rained, the road was slippery”
🔹 No explicit “because” or “and”
🔹 Meaning inferred from order and context
---
## 6. Languages with serial verb constructions
In many African and Southeast Asian languages, **verbs are chained** without conjunctions.
### Yoruba (Nigeria)
⭢ ó lọ ra ìwé
⭢ “he went buy book”
⭢ → “He went and bought a book”
🔹 Action sequence replaces conjunctions
---
## 7. Signed languages
Sign languages express conjunctions using:
* **Facial expressions**
* **Pauses**
* **Hand movement direction**
* **Body shift**
There may be signs for AND / BUT, but often **grammar replaces words**.
---
## 8. Rare or interesting conjunction strategies
### Inclusive vs exclusive “or”
Some languages distinguish:
* **inclusive or** (A or B or both)
* **exclusive or** (A or B but not both)
### Multiple “and” types
Languages may have different “and” depending on:
* animate vs inanimate
* exhaustive vs non-exhaustive lists
---
## Key takeaway
✔ **Conjunction meaning is universal**
❌ **Conjunction words are not**
Languages may use:
* standalone words (English)
* particles (Japanese)
* verb endings (Turkish)
* clause order (Classical Chinese)
* gesture and expression (Sign languages)
---
If you want, I can:
* compare **two specific languages**
* explain conjunctions in **formal logic vs natural language**
* help with **learning conjunctions for a language you’re studying**
* relate this to **programming / logic operators** (which is often fascinating for engineers)"

"In grammar, a conjunction (abbreviated conj or cnj) is a part of speech that connects words, phrases, or clauses that are called the conjuncts of the conjunctions. The term discourse marker is mostly used for conjunctions joining sentences. This definition may overlap with that of other parts of speech, so what constitutes a "conjunction" must be defined for each language. In English a given word may have several senses, being either a preposition or a conjunction depending on the syntax of the sentence (for example, "after" being a preposition in "he left after the fight" versus it being a conjunction in "he left after they fought"). In general, a conjunction is an invariable (noninflected) grammatical particle and it may or may not stand between the items conjoined.
The definition may also be extended to idiomatic phrases that behave as a unit with the same function, e.g. "as well as", "provided that".
A simple literary example of a conjunction: "the truth of nature, and the power of giving interest". (Samuel Taylor Coleridge's Biographia Literaria)[1]
Conjunctions may be placed at the beginning of sentences:[2] "But some superstition about the practice persists".[3]"
[{2019-08-18} https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunction_(grammar)]
